# Entire Graph

Coding agents lose time before the edit, while they are still looking for the
right code. Entire Graph is a plugin for the Entire CLI that gives an agent a
precomputed map of one Git repository: ranked code search plus definitions,
callers, types, routes, and change impact, each with `file:line` locations. The
built-in analyzer parses the repository locally with tree-sitter and makes no
network requests, model calls, or API-key lookups. Installing the plugin is the
networked step.

Setup happens once per repository. After that, the interface is your coding
agent: you ask a code question in plain language, the agent runs graph queries,
reads the code the graph points at, and answers with citations. A captured
example is shown below.

## Benchmarks

The Entire Graph retrieval engine ranked first in an eight-system LoCoMo comparison
(1,540 questions, shared reader and judge, a 200-item retrieval budget requested for
every arm) while building its index without model calls. Measured 2026-08-14 on the
[#104](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/104) branch, before that work merged; the
retrieval path it exercises first shipped in
[v0.4.0](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/releases/tag/v0.4.0) (tagged four days later,
2026-08-18). See § below for what that does and does not license you to claim.

| System | LoCoMo | Index-time tokens | Version tested |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **entire-graph** § | **94.74** | **0** | [#104](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/104) branch, 2026-08-14 (pre-merge) |
| [mem0](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0) | 93.83 | 50.85M | commit [`4debc58`](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0/commit/4debc58a83377b18be81ae1e5969a300736b2fac) |
| [cognee](https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee) | 92.86 | 12.35M | commit [`38eece5`](https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee/commit/38eece5bbb0cb9f5706fed908abd16dba0f5505e) |
| [bm25](https://github.com/dorianbrown/rank_bm25) (lexical baseline) | 91.88 | 0 | [0.2.2](https://github.com/dorianbrown/rank_bm25/releases/tag/0.2.2) |
| [codebase-memory-mcp](https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp) (cmm) † | 91.30 | 0 | [v0.9.0](https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/releases/tag/v0.9.0) |
| [graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify) ¶ | 87.34 | 0 | unpinned — see ¶ |
| [letta](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta) | 84.68 | not projectable | [0.16.8](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/releases/tag/0.16.8) |
| [supermemory](https://github.com/supermemoryai/supermemory) ‡ | 82.08 | hosted | [server-v0.0.7-rc.2](https://github.com/supermemoryai/supermemory/releases/tag/server-v0.0.7-rc.2) |

§ **The 94.74 run is not a measurement of a released tag.** It ran on 2026-08-14 on the #104

never benchmarked. The run id this number comes from, `sw_eg_mr3`, also has **no row in
[`RUN-INDEX.md`](bench/memory/RUN-INDEX.md)**, the registry our own rules require, and the one
registered run that also scores 94.74 (`plan_f_hyb`) used a **non-default** ingest granularity and
is explicitly *not* interchangeable evidence. Quote 94.74 as the #104 branch result, not as v0.4.0's
score. The shipped default at the time, `mrq_base`, scored **91.56**.

¶ **graphify's tested version is not v0.9.43 and is not recoverable.** The run finished 2026-08-14
16:25 UTC; v0.9.43 was published 19:17 UTC the same day — after the run — so it cannot be what was
measured. The checkout no longer exists, so the exact revision cannot be recovered; it was whatever
was current in that window. `UPSTREAM.md` records this as "not a confirmed exact pin".

† **cmm is patched, not stock v0.9.0.** It was modified to emit Markdown sections
([patch](bench/memory/patches/0005-cmm-v0.9.0-markdown-sections.patch)); the linked release alone
does not reproduce 91.30.

‡ **supermemory is patched, and its retrieval budget is half every other row's.** Reaching the
shared extraction model required a binary capability-flag patch plus a wire-level parameter adapter,
and a second fix made its content-dedup tolerate retries. Its search API also hard-caps retrieval at
**100 items where every other arm gets 200** — a disclosed asymmetry that works against
supermemory. The linked release alone does not reproduce 82.08. Full disclosure, including what is
and is not reproducible from this repository:
[`LOCOMO-COMPARISON.md` § ‡](bench/memory/LOCOMO-COMPARISON.md).

See [benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md) for full methodology, per-category results,
retractions, and reproduction steps.

guide](https://docs.entire.io/installation), which also covers Windows and
other channels.

# Parking lot

Deferred work that is intentionally outside the scope of the pull request that
identified it. Each item should be reassessed before implementation so that a
fix does not reduce functionality or performance.

## 1. Validate remaining repository-local structural Git configuration

The broad configuration-derived vectors that motivated this item are now
bounded. Production Git subprocesses disable inherited global and system
configuration; the metadata preflight rejects active repository-local
`[include]` and `[includeIf]` sections and checks active `core.worktree` paths;
protected command-scope `safe.directory` entries retain support for the
explicitly selected directory and its discovery ancestors without using `*`;
and command-scope configuration disables `core.fsmonitor`,
`log.showSignature`, `log.mailmap`, `submodule.recurse`, `core.excludesFile`,
`core.attributesFile`, and `diff.orderFile`. Those fixed settings are no longer
deferred work.

Repository-local structural configuration still cannot be disabled wholesale:
Git needs it for repository format and layout. A follow-up should classify and
preflight the remaining path- or command-bearing settings that the production
command surface can activate. This includes `extensions.refStorage` when it can
name a relocated reftable store, and may include command-bearing settings such as
`core.alternateRefsCommand` as command coverage evolves. The follow-up must
preserve supported repository formats, the provider's no-egress contract, and
current performance; it should not re-list neutralized settings as unresolved.

## 3. Enforce metadata validation at the Git subprocess boundary

Production entrypoints currently perform the required repository metadata
validation before launching Git, but the shared Git command constructors do not
enforce it. A future caller could omit the guard, and repository metadata can
also change between validation and a later Git operation.

A deterministic test now confirms the remaining race: after a successful
validation, replacing a checked metadata entry before command construction lets
the Git subprocess start. Repeating the pathname check closer to launch would
only narrow that window, not close it, so it is not a complete correction.

A follow-up should move enforcement to the shared subprocess boundary, ideally
using held handles or a synthetic/index-only environment where practical. This
likely requires relocating validator and rooted-path helpers into a lower-level
package, along with their platform-specific tests. The design must avoid import
cycles while preserving no-egress guarantees, functionality, and performance.

## 4. Harden dependent-file fallback coordinates for future subdirectory callers

The dependent-file helper passes scope-relative paths to `LimitedFileReader`,
whose contract uses paths rooted at Git's command tree. The current production
caller first normalizes the repository to `RepoCommandRoot`, so its scope prefix
is empty and the mismatch is not reachable in shipped behavior. A direct or
future subdirectory caller could nevertheless undercount dependents when the
batch reader falls back to bounded individual reads.

If such a caller is added, compute the repository prefix once and apply it only
to `LimitedFileReader.Prime` and `LimitedFileReader.ReadFile`; keep the original
scope-relative paths for batch reads, parsing, and diagnostics. Preserve the
current two-batch behavior for newline-bearing candidates and avoid adding work
to the normalized production path until the helper contract actually changes.

# Command reference

Day to day, Entire Graph is driven by a coding agent following the guide that
`init-agents` installs. The commands below are the same surface used directly
for manual inspection, debugging a result the agent acted on, or scripting.
`entire graph help` lists every public command for your installed version, and
`entire graph <command> --help` is authoritative for flags; this page groups
the commands by task and records the defaults that matter most.

Pass `--repo .` (or a path) when running outside an Entire session.

## Set up

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `init-agents` | Writes `.entire/graph-agent.md` and managed blocks in `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`. See [agent activation](agents.md). |
| `agent-guide` | Prints the operating guide `init-agents` installs, for inspection or piping elsewhere. |
| `index` | Prewarms one committed-tree cache variant before a batch of `--head` queries. Defaults to `--profile full`; see the [operations cache guide](operations.md#cache). |
| `capabilities` | Reports semantic vs inventory-only languages, relation types, profiles, and features as JSON. Feature-detect with this before relying on a relation family. |

## Inspect

These five form the interactive query family. They read the **working tree by
default**; `--head` switches to the committed tree.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `search` | Ranked source regions for a plain-language query. Defaults: `--format json`, `--profile fast` (the installed agent guide asks for `--profile full`). Formats: `json`, `ndjson`, `text`, `agent`. See [search results](search.md). |
| `def` | One name's declaration, fields, and method surface. Default format is text. |
| `explain` | Resolves symbols named by a failing build or test into definitions and context. |
| `neighbors` | Direct relations of one symbol (`--relation`, `--direction`, `--depth 1\|2`). Ambiguous names return a definition list; disambiguate with `--file`. |
| `impact` | One-shot blast radius for a symbol: direct and transitive callers (depth ≤ 2), callees, type consumers, data flows, co-change files, siblings. |

Cache visibility differs by command and format. JSON from `search`, `impact`,
and `neighbors` includes cache fields. Text output from `impact` and
`neighbors` starts with an `Index: cache-hit` or `cache-miss` header. Agent
output from `search` and `neighbors` normally uses that header, compacting it
to `I:hit`/`I:miss` under a tight byte budget and potentially omitting it under
an extreme cap. `search --format text` and `explain` report no cache state.
`def` and `explain` also skip the per-user fallback cache directory that the
other query commands use; details are in the
[operations cache guide](operations.md#cache).

## Analyze changes

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `commit <ref>` | Entity-level change list for a commit vs its first parent, with heuristic dependent counts. |
| `diff --base A --head B` | The same between two refs. `analyze` is an alias of `diff`. |
| `checkpoint <id>` | Analyzes the commit behind an Entire-Checkpoint trailer. |
| `verify` | Runs a caller-provided test command and returns an adjudicated verdict. This executes the command you pass it; see [trust and security](trust-and-security.md). |

## Export

Bulk NDJSON streams. These default to the **committed tree**; pass
`--worktree` to stream the working tree instead.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `snapshot` | The whole graph: header, files, externals, symbols, relations, summary. Also supports `--format compact-ndjson` and the experimental `--format scip`. |
| `symbols` | Symbol records only. There is no name filter; grep the stream, or use `search`/`def` for a targeted lookup. |
| `edges` | Relation records, filterable server-side with `--to`, `--from`, `--relation`. |
| `snapshot-query` | Queries a saved compact snapshot without rebuilding the graph. |

Stream and record formats are specified in
[snapshot format](snapshot-format.md).

## Report

`stats` is a human-facing, read-only report of graph vs grep/read usage in
local coding-agent transcripts, with an explicitly modeled (not measured)
token-savings estimate. It is not part of the agent workflow; see
[trust and security](trust-and-security.md) for what it reads.

## Codex removal

**Removed:** the outer folder's `.codex/` (7 Entire Codex hooks that `entire enable --agent codex` installed by mistake). `entire status` in `Scaler Buildathon/` now reports `Agents · Claude Code` only.

Those are **tracked upstream files that ship as part of the plugin** (it supports Codex users), sitting right next to the Claude equivalents in [.claude/](entire-graph-deathcode/.claude/) and [.claude-plugin/](entire-graph-deathcode/.claude-plugin/). Deleting them would put unrelated product deletions in your Buildathon diff. They are also inert here — `codex` isn't installed on this machine. Optional: the outer `Scaler Buildathon/` folder is an accidental empty git repo with a stray `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` (the file open in your IDE right now is that stray copy, not the project's). To clean it: `rm -rf "/Users/arhan/1. New Study Material/Scaler Buildathon/.git" .entire .claude AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md`. I left it alone because your current session's Entire hooks live there.

## What the project actually is

`entire-graph-deathcode` is your fork of **entire-graph v0.4.0** — a mature Go 1.26 plugin for the Entire CLI, ~20 supported languages, tree-sitter based, zero network calls. Not a starter template. Verified: builds clean, on `main`, remote is your fork `arenforge/entire-graph-deathcode`, checkpoints sync to origin.

Architecture:

| Layer | Location |
|---|---|
| Binary entrypoint | [cmd/entire-graph/](entire-graph-deathcode/cmd/entire-graph/) |
| Command dispatch (one big switch, 25 commands) | [internal/cli/root.go:72-125](entire-graph-deathcode/internal/cli/root.go#L72-L125) |
| Query commands | `search.go`, `def.go`, `explain.go`, `neighbors.go`, `impact.go` |
| Change analysis | `diff`/`commit`/`checkpoint` → `analyze` path |
| Semantic engine + per-language extractors | [internal/sem/](entire-graph-deathcode/internal/sem/) (~100 files, one per language) |
| Markdown report rendering | [internal/cli/report.go](entire-graph-deathcode/internal/cli/report.go) |
| Docs (excellent — read these) | [docs/commands.md](entire-graph-deathcode/docs/commands.md), [docs/search.md](entire-graph-deathcode/docs/search.md), [docs/parking-lot.md](entire-graph-deathcode/docs/parking-lot.md) |

The bar is high: roughly 60% of `internal/cli` is tests, there are 4 ADRs, a LoCoMo benchmark harness, and the README self-discloses its own benchmark caveats. Judges will expect your addition to match that standard — implementation *plus* tests *plus* docs.

1. **Work only in the nested folder.** `cd "/Users/arhan/1. New Study Material/Scaler Buildathon/entire-graph-deathcode"`
2. **Establish a green baseline before anyone edits** (takes a few minutes, don't skip — you need to know failures are yours):

The pieces already exist separately — `diff` gives changed entities but only *heuristic dependent counts*, `impact` gives blast radius for *one symbol at a time*, and nothing maps a change to its covering tests. Composing them is a real gap, it's the tool's own thesis applied to itself, and it demos in 30 seconds. It also splits cleanly four ways:

- **P3:** the risk/coverage logic in `internal/sem/`, reusing `dependents.go` and the diff path
- **P4:** tests, `docs/commands.md` entry, README example, demo script

BTW Buildathon 2026 - Participant Guide


Buildathon 2026 Participant Guide


This is your operating guide for the Bengaluru Tech Week Buildathon. Read it before arrival, keep it open during the build, and use the final checklist before you submit. The submission deadline is 3:00 PM IST.

Your day
Time

What happens

What you should do

8:00–9:00

Breakfast, check-in and setup

Arrive early. Confirm your team, laptop, power, GitHub access, development tools and optional Databricks Free Edition access.

9:00–12:00

Kickoff and build session

Choose one Entire track, fork only after the official start, configure the required Entire workflow, build a narrow end-to-end slice and create your early checkpoints.

12:00–1:00

The Noon Curveball and lunch

Stop, preserve your last stable version, close the current agent session, receive the new constraint, start fresh and reconstruct the project from checkpoint context before editing.

1:00–3:00

Build session and submission

Implement the constraint, test the changed behavior, verify the Entire Graph evidence, create the final checkpoint, finish BUILDATHON.md and submit before 3:00 PM.

3:00–5:00

Judging and winner announcement

Keep the project runnable. Mentors complete first-level review; eight finalists present; judges deliberate and awards are announced.


What makes this Buildathon different
You are not being asked to produce a generic app around a prompt. You must build a useful developer product on one of three Entire open-source surfaces, preserve decision context through checkpoints, use structural evidence from the Entire Graph where required, and respond to an additional non-negotiable constraint revealed at noon.

Teams may also make Databricks essential to the same product and opt in to the separate Best Use of Databricks awards. There remains one project and one submission; a team may win both an Entire main-challenge prize and a Databricks award.

Before you arrive
Bring and verify
A laptop, charger and any adapters you need. Bring a power bank only as a backup; do not rely on it for the full day.
A working GitHub account with permission to create forks and push to your fork.
Your preferred coding agent and local development tools already installed and signed in.
A local runtime that can run tests and a browser or API client that can demonstrate the product.
A Databricks Free Edition account if your team wants to compete for Best Use of Databricks. Create and open it before the event so account issues do not consume your build window.
A fallback demo asset: a recent screenshot or short screen recording for any step that depends on a live service.
Allowed before 9:00 AM
Research, user discovery, problem framing, sketches and planning are allowed before the official start. Implementation must begin after 9:00 AM on 6 September. Do not arrive with a prebuilt solution, completed feature branch or reusable implementation that gives your team an unfair head start.

Team readiness
Name one person as submission owner. This person checks every link and submits before 3:00 PM.
Name one person as the final demo owner. They should be able to explain the system even if another teammate wrote most of the code.
If using Databricks, choose one final demo workspace and one deployment owner. Use Git for shared code; never store secrets in the repository.
Agree how you will record decisions, failures and verified outcomes in checkpoints and BUILDATHON.md.
Account links
Create or open Databricks Free Edition

Buildathon details and updates

Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct







Choose one Entire innovation track
Your team must select one track. The project should solve a real developer or agent-workflow problem and make Entire essential to the solution. Adding Entire only for tracking, without using its context, checkpoints or graph evidence to improve the product, will not qualify.

Track 1 — Build a Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience
Repository: Entire CLI

Build a developer tool or workflow powered by context preserved in Entire Checkpoints. Git shows what changed; checkpoints should preserve why a change happened, what the agent attempted, which assumptions were made, what failed and what remains unresolved.

Review an implementation against its stated intent.
Identify unfinished requirements or unresolved risks.
Create a change-risk or release-readiness report.
Hand work to another developer or agent without losing the original reasoning.
Resume an agent-assisted workflow with confidence after a break.
Success looks like this: checkpoint context is an essential input, and a developer or agent completes a useful task more accurately or efficiently than they could from a Git diff alone.

Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence
Repository: Entire Graph

Use the Entire Graph’s structural view of a codebase to support a useful decision or action. The graph can surface definitions, call relationships, types, routes and semantic changes. Your product must turn that evidence into a workflow that a developer or agent can inspect and verify.

Impact-aware code review or change-risk analysis.
Test selection based on affected relationships.
Migration planning or dependency-aware refactoring.
Codebase onboarding and guided exploration.
Combining Entire Graph findings with checkpoint intent.
Raw graph output is not enough. Your product should produce a useful decision, recommendation or workflow, show where the evidence came from, and let the user verify it against source code or tests.

Track 3 — Bring Entire to a New Agent or Workflow
Repository: Entire External Agents

Extend or create an Entire integration for a coding agent, editor, development environment, CI process or software-delivery workflow. The integration must capture meaningful development context and keep working in its intended operating mode.

Support for a new coding agent or editor workflow.
A CI or pull-request workflow that uses checkpoint context.
A multi-agent coordination workflow.
A protocol adapter between Entire and another developer tool.
External SDKs and fixtures are allowed, but the submitted implementation must live in the designated Entire fork. Calling an Entire command from another interface is not sufficient by itself.


Required Entire workflow
Complete these steps after the 9:00 AM kickoff. All implementation must happen in the clone created through the Entire mirror workflow.

1. Fork your selected repository
Fork the repository associated with your chosen track only after the Buildathon begins. Use existing issues for inspiration, or propose an original feature, integration or workflow.

2. Sign in and create the mirror
entire login

entire repo mirror create

entire repo clone /gh/YOUR-GITHUB-HANDLE/REPOSITORY

Select your fork and the India region when prompted. Clone through Entire, then work inside that clone.

3. Enable checkpoints
entire enable -y --agent YOUR-BUILD-AGENT

entire status

Commit meaningful milestones so code and context remain connected. Your checkpoint history must include at least:

Initial understanding and intended architecture.
The last stable state before the Noon Curveball.
Your response to the Noon Curveball.
Final implementation and verification.
Checkpoint quality matters more than quantity. Capture decisions, rejected options, failures, assumptions, open risks and the evidence that changed your approach.

4. Activate Entire Graph
entire plugin install graph

entire graph version

entire graph init-agents --repo .

Start a fresh agent session after activation so the agent receives the graph instructions. During development, show at least:

A graph search or definition lookup.
A relationship or impact analysis before a high-risk change.
A final semantic diff analysis of the submitted implementation.
Graph results are evidence, not an oracle. Verify findings against source code, tests and runtime behavior. Never present incomplete or uncertain graph output as a fact.


The Noon Curveball
At exactly 12:00 noon, every team receives an additional track-specific constraint that becomes mandatory. The first version is the proof of what you built. The second version is the proof that your process can absorb change without losing intent.

11:45 AM — preserve the stable state
Stop adding optional features and get the product back to a runnable state.
Commit the last stable version.
Create the required pre-noon Entire Checkpoint.
Record the current intent, architecture, completed work, unresolved work and important technical risks.
12:00 PM — receive the constraint
Stop implementation and close the current coding-agent session.
Receive the official Curveball from the organising team. Do not exchange cards or use another track’s instruction.
Start a fresh agent session and use checkpoint context to reconstruct the project before editing.
Run Entire Graph impact analysis before changing the affected area.
Implement the smallest complete response, test it and record the result in a new checkpoint.
What judges will look for
A strong response preserves the product’s core idea, changes a real architectural or reliability decision, uses checkpoint context accurately, uses graph evidence where relevant, remains testable and explains why the revised behavior can be trusted.

The Curveball’s specific instructions are intentionally not published in advance. Mentors and organisers must not disclose them before noon.


Competing for Best Use of Databricks
Databricks is an additional award category within the same project.

Free Edition setup
Each teammate may explore in an individual Databricks Free Edition workspace.
Choose one final workspace for the shared dataset, deployed app or endpoint and final demonstration.
Keep notebooks, app code, configuration and documentation in the shared Git repository. Never commit access tokens or credentials.
Name one deployment owner and test that the owner can sign in and open every required resource before judging.
Good scope for a one-day build
An AI app or agent using Databricks Apps, hosted foundation models, model serving or AI Search where available.
An analytics experience using notebooks, SQL, dashboards or Genie to answer a concrete question.
A data pipeline that ingests, cleans and transforms representative data into a useful result.
A data-backed application using Lakehouse data and Databricks Apps for the user experience.
An ML experiment that uses a reproducible dataset, experiment tracking and an evaluation result.
Free Edition constraints to design around
Area

Planning constraint

Service model

No-cost, serverless, quota-limited environment for non-commercial learning and prototyping; no production SLA.

SQL and jobs

One serverless 2X-Small SQL warehouse; up to five concurrent job tasks per account.

Pipelines

One active pipeline per supported pipeline type.

Models and AI Search

Endpoint, throughput and model availability limits apply; no GPU or provisioned throughput; AI Search is limited.

Apps and database

Up to three Apps, with idle auto-stop behavior; one Lakebase project where available.

Workspace

One workspace and one metastore per account; several account-level and enterprise controls are unavailable.

Quota

When quota is exhausted, affected compute may be unavailable for the rest of the day or month. Build and test your narrow path early.


Work locally when practical, deploy one narrow slice early and preserve a screenshot or recording of any fragile live step. If live infrastructure fails during judging, explain the expected behavior, show the prepared evidence and continue with the product story.

Databricks Free Edition overview

Current Databricks Free Edition limitations

Responsible use of AI and data
Do not upload confidential company information, customer data, passwords, private keys or personal data that you do not have permission to use.
Do not put secrets in prompts, source repositories, screenshots, checkpoint context or BUILDATHON.md.
Verify generated code, SQL, citations and outputs. Test the cases that matter to your user and disclose what remains unverified.
Explain your data sources, permitted use, sampling or transformation, and important limitations.
Clearly label synthetic, cached, mocked or prototype data and responses.
You remain accountable for the implementation, even when a coding agent created it. Every teammate presenting should understand the relevant code and product decisions.
Final 20-minute checklist
The final commit is pushed and the SHA matches the submission.
The project launches from a clean checkout or the documented setup path.
Required checkpoints open and clearly explain the four milestones.
Entire Graph evidence and the final semantic-diff analysis are recorded.

Read the Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct

Selected Entire track.

`entire graph review` turns a commit range into a reviewable change-risk
verdict: every changed symbol, its blast radius, the tests that actually cover
it, and an explicit list of changes that nothing covers — each claim carrying a
`file:line` citation the reviewer can open.

## Problem, intended user and why it matters

The user is a developer reviewing a change an agent wrote. A Git diff answers
"what text moved". It does not answer the question that decides whether the
change is safe to merge: *what else depends on this, and is any of it tested?*
Today that requires running `entire graph impact` once per changed symbol and
correlating the results by hand. On an agent-authored change touching a dozen
symbols, nobody does that, so untested blast radius ships.

## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential

**Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence.**

The product cannot exist without the graph. Mapping a changed line to the
symbol that contains it, that symbol to its transitive callers, and those
callers to the test functions that reach them is a call-graph query, not a text
query. Entire Graph supplies it locally, with no model calls, and returns
`file:line` for every node — which is what makes the verdict auditable instead
of advisory.
